description: Question: Hardy–Weinberg says that under random mating an allele at frequency p comes in genotypes p², 2pq and q², whatever p is. Do real human populations follow it, and what does it mean when they don't? Data: genotype counts for five well-known variants (rs4988235 lactase persistence, rs1426654 SLC24A5 skin pigmentation, rs671 ALDH2 alcohol flush, rs1815739 ACTN3 R577X, rs334 sickle-cell HbS) in the 26 populations of 1000 Genomes phase 3 (Ensembl REST), and the populations' sampling sites and super-populations (IGSR). Steps: per variant and sample, the allele frequency, the expected genotype counts, a chi-square test (1 df) and the heterozygote deficit F = 1 − H_obs/H_exp; then the Wahlund effect: for each pooled sample (all 26, or one super-population) the deficit predicted from the populations alone, F_ST = Var(p) / (p̄(1 − p̄)). Aha: single populations sit on the Hardy–Weinberg parabola (3 of 83 population tests at p < 0.05, all for ACTN3, about what chance gives), but pooling them makes heterozygotes vanish: all 2,504 people together have F = 0.67 for SLC24A5 (408 heterozygotes where 1,232 are expected), 0.39 for LCT and 0.20 for ALDH2, and F_ST from the populations predicts 0.65, 0.36 and 0.18. A departure from Hardy–Weinberg is a clue, not an error: here it is structure (a pooled sample is not one mating population). HbS goes the other way: no homozygotes among 661 Africans where 6.6 are expected (F = −0.11, p = 0.004), the mark of selection (sickle-cell disease against malaria protection for carriers), which in the pooled ALL sample cancels the Wahlund deficit (F = −0.03). Caveats: the variants were chosen for being famous, not at random; 61–113 people per population give the tests little power and some expected counts under 5; genotype calls have errors; sampling sites are where people were sampled (CEU in Utah). Next: hover any dot; add any rsID as another query; drill down to one super-population's populations; expand to selection scans or ancient DNA.
name: Hardy–Weinberg, and why pooled populations break it
